analysis.one_liner: Requires drug manufacturers to pay Medicare rebates on drugs dispensed to low-income beneficiaries.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee markup or floor vote in the Senate and died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required prescription drug manufacturers to pay the federal government rebates on drugs dispensed to low-income Medicare beneficiaries — roughly the same rebates companies already must pay under Medicaid. Manufacturers that refused would have had their drugs excluded from Medicare Part D coverage. The rebates would be deposited into the Medicare prescription drug account, reducing federal drug spending. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers and the Medicare program would gain, because manufacturer rebates on drugs used by low-income enrollees would be deposited into Medicare's prescription drug account [S3]. Low-income beneficiaries — people eligible for both Medicare and Medicaid or receiving low-income subsidies — would benefit because their drugs would cost Medicare far less, freeing program resources; they themselves would pay nothing extra [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires drug manufacturers to pay the Secretary of Health and Human Services a rebate, calculated using the Medicaid rebate formula, for each covered Part D drug dispensed to a rebate-eligible (low-income) individual, with payment made through private Part D plans or Medicare Advantage plans [S2][S3].
Excludes any drug from Medicare Part D coverage if its manufacturer refuses to sign a rebate agreement, giving companies a strong incentive to participate [S2][S3].
Deposits all rebate payments into the Medicare Prescription Drug Account, meaning the savings go back into the Medicare program rather than to private intermediaries [S3].

Requires Part D plan sponsors to report utilization and price-concession data to manufacturers and the government, with civil money penalties ($10,000 per day for late data, up to $100,000 per false item) to enforce compliance, and makes the data available to the HHS Inspector General for audits [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would bear the cost, paying government rebates on every unit dispensed to low-income Medicare enrollees — the same population over which Medicaid already imposes rebates. Part D plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage organizations would take on new data-reporting duties, though the actual money flows from manufacturers.

drawbacks.text: The rebate is structured as the amount by which the Medicaid rebate exceeds the average discount plans already negotiate, so it targets the gap between Medicaid pricing and Medicare Part D pricing; manufacturers argued that layering government-mandated rebates on top of private negotiations reduces the returns that fund research on new medicines and could lead companies to raise launch prices on new drugs.

Part D plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage organizations would face new reporting obligations on drug utilization and price concessions for every low-income enrollee, with civil money penalties for late or false data — administrative work that private plans would pass on in their bids.

The bill excludes the new rebates from the Medicaid 'best price' and average manufacturer price calculations, an accounting carve-out that adds complexity to how drug prices are measured across the two programs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: drug companies would give up some revenue on drugs sold to low-income Medicare enrollees, and Medicare would keep that money instead. Low-income beneficiaries pay nothing extra, and the strongest honest objection is about incentives — manufacturers claimed that mandated rebates shrink the profits that fund drug development. The design mirrors the Medicaid rebate system that has operated since 1990, so the mechanism is well-tested rather than experimental, but the administrative reporting load on private plans is real.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never held a markup or vote on it, and it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Sen. John Rockefeller introduced the bill on June 15, 2011, with 13 cosponsors (12 Democrats and 1 Independent) including Sens. Bingaman, Stabenow, Blumenthal, Brown, Boxer, Franken, and Merkley [S1][S4][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that was the last action ever taken on the bill [S5].
No markup, hearing vote, committee report, or floor vote followed during the remainder of the 112th Congress, and the bill expired on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers are better off, since the bill died before it could impose Medicaid-style rebates on drugs dispensed to low-income Medicare enrollees. No one on the public side gained from the outcome.

for.name: Sen. John D. Rockefeller IV
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Medicare Drug Savings Act of 2011 and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor

for.name: 13 senators (12 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.role: Cosponsors, including Sens. Bingaman, Stabenow, Blumental, Brown of Ohio, Boxer, Franken, and Merkley

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred, chaired by Sen. Max Baucus (D-MT)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; it died in committee when the Congress ended

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA) and brand-name drug manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Opposed extending Medicaid-style government rebates to Medicare Part D beneficiaries, the position the bill would have enforced

sides.party_line_note: All 14 sponsors were Democrats or the Independent who caucuses with Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced past referral to the Democratic-led Finance Committee.

industries.note: The bill would force them to pay Medicaid-style government rebates on every drug dispensed to low-income Medicare enrollees, and to have their products excluded from Part D entirely if they refuse. Their gain in blocking it is revenue the Medicare program would otherwise have reclaimed.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage insurers
industries.note: Plans would have had to collect and report detailed utilization and price-concession data to manufacturers and the government, with fines for failures, but the actual rebate money would come from manufacturers, not from the plans.

The rebate formula follows Medicaid rules, which set lower rebates for non-innovator multiple source drugs; generics would owe smaller rebates, and any pressure toward lower drug prices generally favors lower-cost substitutes.
